facts.raw_span: bilateral ventriculomegaly with dilation of both frontal and occipital horns
multiple hyperechoic regions with indistinct margins within the ventricular lumens
areas of high signal intensity on T1-weighted images and low signal intensity on T2-weighted images within the ventricles

a comprehensive workup—including a TORCH panel, platelet count, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, plasminogen levels, von Willebrand factor, factor V Leiden, protein S, protein C, and antiplatelet antibodies—returned within normal limits

concepts.why: Bilateral ventriculomegaly and ventricular enlargement are indicative of congenital hydrocephalus.
The presence of bilateral ventriculomegaly with dilation of both frontal and occipital horns and irregular ventricular walls supports this diagnosis.
Although the TORCH panel returned within normal limits, the possibility of an intrauterine infection cannot be entirely ruled out.
The comprehensive workup including coagulation tests returned within normal limits, but fetal coagulopathy is still a consideration.
It explains the roughened-appearing choroid plexus and areas of high signal intensity on T1-weighted images and low signal intensity on T2-weighted images within the ventricles.

rationales.F05: Bilateral ventriculomegaly is a key feature of Congenital Hydrocephalus and Fetal Ventriculomegaly.
rationales.F07: Multiple hyperechoic regions within the ventricular lumens may indicate hemorrhage or other pathology, supporting Fetal Intraventricular Hemorrhage.
rationales.F11: Areas of high signal intensity on T1-weighted images and low signal intensity on T2-weighted images within the ventricles may indicate hemorrhage or other pathology, supporting Fetal Intraventricular Hemorrhage.
rationales.F12: A comprehensive workup with normal results helps rule out Intrauterine Infection and Fetal Coagulopathy.

frontier_selector.rationale: Bilateral ventriculomegaly with dilation of both frontal and occipital horns, irregular ventricular walls, and multiple hyperechoic regions within the ventricular lumens support Fetal Ventriculomegaly, which is a more specific diagnosis than Congenital Hydrocephalus.
